config.title: Write polling with start stop and backoff

intro.title: Write polling with start stop and backoff
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a polling mechanism that can start, stop, and automatically back off when encountering errors. You will learn how to use JavaScript's setInterval and clearInterval to control periodic data fetching. The core concept involves managing state for the polling interval and implementing exponential backoff logic to handle failures gracefully. You'll work with functions, conditionals, and state variables to create a robust polling utility.
intro.usecase: Polling with start/stop and backoff is essential for real-time data updates in production applications. You'll implement this pattern in dashboard widgets that refresh stock prices or server metrics, where users need current information but excessive requests must be avoided. It's also used in notification systems that check for new messages while respecting server limits with exponential backoff delays. This approach balances live data needs with system performance and reliability.

objectives: Initialize a polling interval with configurable timing parameters
Implement start and stop functions to control polling execution
Apply exponential backoff logic to adjust polling intervals dynamically
Configure error handling to trigger backoff mechanisms
Integrate state management to track polling status and interval data
Manipulate DOM elements to display real-time polling results
Construct a complete polling system with user controls for start, stop, and reset

steps.title: Import required modules
steps.instruction: Import the required modules for the polling implementation. You'll need to import React and the useState hook from 'react'.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and useState from the 'react' package.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: importing React and a hook
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The imports are added at the top of the file, enabling the use of React and state in the polling component.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've imported something, but check if both React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The imports are missing or incorrect. Ensure you import React and useState from 'react'.

steps.title: Create main polling function
steps.instruction: Create a function named 'startPolling' that will handle the polling logic. The function should take no parameters and return nothing for now.
steps.hint: Define a function using either 'function startPolling() {}' or 'const startPolling = () => {}'.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';
// Create the startPolling function here
steps.expectedOutcome: A function named 'startPolling' is defined in your code.
successCriteria: The function 'startPolling' is defined with an empty body.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the function is named exactly 'startPolling'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function wasn't created correctly. Please define a function named 'startPolling'.

steps.title: Initialize polling state variables
steps.instruction: Inside your component, initialize three state variables: one to track if polling is active (boolean), one to store the current polling interval (number), and one to store the fetched data (string or null).
steps.hint: Use useState to create three separate state variables with appropriate initial values.
steps.expectedOutcome: Three state variables are initialized with appropriate names and initial values.
successCriteria: State variables for polling status (boolean), interval (number), and data (string/null) are declared with useState.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've initialized some state variables, but check if you have all three: polling status (boolean), interval (number), and data (string or null).
steps.feedbackWrong: The state variables aren't properly initialized. Make sure to use useState for all three variables with appropriate initial values.

steps.title: Define the fetch data function
steps.instruction: Inside your component, create a function named fetchData that makes a fetch call to 'https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/1' and logs the response.
steps.hint: Use the fetch API with async/await or .then() to get data from the URL.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a fetchData function that can be called to retrieve data from an API endpoint.
successCriteria: A function named fetchData is defined that uses fetch to call the API URL and logs the response.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your function is named fetchData and includes a fetch call to the correct URL.
steps.feedbackWrong: The fetchData function is missing or doesn't match the requirements. Check the function name and fetch call.

steps.title: Implement stop polling function
steps.instruction: Create a function named stopPolling that clears the active polling interval.
steps.hint: Inside the function, use clearInterval to stop the interval stored in your polling state variable.
steps.expectedOutcome: A stopPolling function is defined that clears the polling interval when called.
successCriteria: The stopPolling function is implemented and uses clearInterval on the interval ID variable.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your stopPolling function actually calls clearInterval with the correct interval ID variable.
steps.feedbackWrong: The stopPolling function is missing or doesn't properly clear the interval. Review how to use clearInterval to stop polling.

steps.title: Add backoff mechanism
steps.instruction: Inside your polling function, add logic to double the polling interval when a request fails,
steps.hint: You can check if the fetch was successful, then adjust the currentInterval variable accordingly.
steps.expectedOutcome: The polling function will now implement exponential backoff, increasing the interval after failures and resetting after successes.
successCriteria: The code includes logic that doubles the interval on failed requests and resets to base interval on successful requests.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some backoff logic, but make sure to handle both success (reset to base interval) and failure (double interval) cases.
steps.feedbackWrong: The backoff mechanism isn't implemented correctly. Review how to adjust the interval based on request success/failure.

steps.title: Create UI structure
steps.instruction: Return the JSX structure for your polling demo, including a wrapper div, a heading, buttons for start and stop, and a paragraph to display data.
steps.hint: Start by returning a div element that contains an h1, two buttons, and a p tag. Use the state variables you've created for button labels and data display.
steps.expectedOutcome: A functional component that returns a complete UI structure with heading, buttons, and data display area.
successCriteria: The component returns JSX containing a div wrapper, an h1 heading, two button elements, and a paragraph element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You have some elements, but make sure to include all required parts: a wrapper div, heading, two buttons, and a paragraph for data display.
steps.feedbackWrong: The UI structure is incomplete or missing. Please ensure you return JSX with a div wrapper containing an h1, two buttons, and a p element.

steps.title: Wire start and stop buttons to polling functions
steps.instruction: Add onClick event handlers to the start and stop buttons that call your startPolling and stopPolling functions respectively.
steps.hint: Use the onClick attribute on each button element and pass the corresponding function name without parentheses.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: wiring a button to a handler
<button onClick={handleClick}>Click me</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: The start and stop buttons will be connected to their respective polling functions, making them interactive.
successCriteria: Both buttons have onClick handlers that call the correct polling functions.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some event handlers, but check that both buttons are correctly connected.
steps.feedbackWrong: The buttons aren't properly connected yet. Make sure each button has an onClick handler calling the right function.

steps.title: Display polling status and data
steps.instruction: Update the paragraph that shows the polling status to display the current status from your state variable and include the fetched data when available.

Status: {status} - Data: {data ? JSON.stringify(data) : 'No data yet'}
steps.expectedOutcome: The UI will dynamically show the current polling status and any fetched data instead of static text.
successCriteria: The paragraph displays the polling status from state and includes fetched data when available.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've updated the status display, but make sure to also include the fetched data when available.
steps.feedbackWrong: The status paragraph still shows static text. Update it to use your state variables for status and data.
